To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
EEG epoch selection should consider alpha rhythm, because EEG epochs with rare alpha content discriminate Alzheimer's disease better.
EEG epochs with poor AR (RAS) are better than those with richer AR (DAS) to discriminate mild-AD from controls.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a new epoch selection method that could be used in AD diagnosis.
the selection of EEG epochs for classification of mild AD.
a new approach for epoch selection, which is crucial to obtain reliable results in EEG studies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the case of AD, EEG epoch selection is more effective with RAS than with DAS, and that the RAS scenario is more effective than DAS in discriminating AD.
EEG epochs presenting poor alpha rhythm are more informative than those presenting richer AR, in terms of discriminating AD from healthy controls, and this is the first study showing this effect.
, for the mild AD EEG data, RAS epochs are more discriminative than DAS epochs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
EEG epochs with poor or no alpha rhythm are better for the discrimination of mild AD patients than those with rich alpha.
the lack of alpha rhythm is a better marker than alpha abundance to distinguish mild AD patients from healthy subjects, and that EEG epoch selection should be based on alpha rhythm.
EEG epochs with scarce alpha rhythm are the best to discriminate mild AD patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
EEG epoch selection should be done carefully and that alpha rhythm is not always a good indicator of cognitive impairment.
, in EEG epoch selection, the presence of alpha rhythm is not always a desirable characteristic.
EEG epoch selection is a crucial step in the analysis of EEG data and that it must be performed with great care.
